channel.title: TaskIAP field notes
channel.description: Field notes on construction project management.

item.title: Done Should Be Calculated, Not Typed
item.description: On most status reports, done is a number somebody types. It drifts up, because nobody wants the argument, and then sits at 95 percent for months (the last 5 percent).

item.title: Every Open Item Should Explain Itself
item.description: Ask why a task isn't finished and the answer usually takes three phone calls. The crew is waiting on scaffold. Scaffold is waiting on a permit. The permit is waiting on a signature from someone on…

item.title: Price Every Risk in Days
item.description: A heat map puts a risk in a red square. It doesn't say what the risk would do to the finish date, so the meeting argues about colours.

item.title: A Crane Is a Predecessor Too
item.description: Two lifts that need the same crane can't happen at once. That tie is as firm as rebar before concrete. Most schedules keep logic in one place and resources in another, and reconcile them at the…

item.title: Write the Site Rules Once
item.description: No hot work within 10 metres of fuel. Two people for confined space entry. Hold for the inspector before backfill. These rules are in a binder, a toolbox talk and the superintendent's head. The…

item.title: The Last 5 Percent
item.description: Punch lists, commissioning, turnover documents and closeout often take a third of the calendar. They get planned as if they were the last 5 percent of the work, and they start getting managed when…

item.title: Keep the As-Built Schedule
item.description: At closeout, the start and finish of every activity gets archived with the project files and is never opened again. It is the best estimating data a contractor owns: real production rates, on its…

item.title: The Cost of Asking
item.description: Every site has a price for asking a question. Part of it is time: finding the person who knows, then waiting for them to answer. Part of it is social: looking like you should already know. When the…

item.title: Count the Handoffs
item.description: Schedules count tasks. Most of what goes wrong happens between tasks, where work, information or authority passes from one person, crew, company or system to the next.

item.title: How Long Bad News Takes to Reach the Plan
item.description: Every problem has two dates: when someone on site first saw it, and when it showed up in the plan. Call the gap bad-news latency. On most jobs it runs to days or weeks, and for all of that time…

item.title: Inside Jokes Are a Good Sign
item.description: A crew that draws cartoons on the trailer whiteboard is a crew that talks. The GIF about the sticking valve in Sector 4 does more to keep people away from that valve than the line in last month's…

item.title: Put Odd People Where They Fit
item.description: The person who annoys everyone by checking every bolt callout is the one who catches the wrong grade before the pour. The one who argues in every meeting is the one asking what happens when the…

item.title: Most Problem Employees Are Reacting to the Job
item.description: Give someone who looks checked out a ready work front, the right tools and a straight answer when they ask, and most of them start working well. A lot of bad attitudes are reasonable responses to a…

item.title: Match the Rigour to the Consequence
item.description: A temporary laydown pad does not need the paperwork of a pressure boundary. Spending four days perfecting it costs four days on work that drives the finish.

item.title: Give Instructions With Tolerances
item.description: Drawings say ±5 mm. Instructions say "ASAP". The crew can't tell a hold point from a favour, so they treat everything as urgent and get worn out by work that wasn't.

item.title: Define the Activity, Not Just Its Duration
item.description: "Hydrovac the copper lines, 3 days" invites three days of digging whether you need it or not. "Hydrovac until you can see the layout, a day at most" tells the crew when they're done.

item.title: Check Your Float
item.description: Float is only as good as the logic under it. One missing tie and an activity shows eight days of slack it doesn't have. One padded duration and a path looks critical when it isn't.

item.title: Not All Milestones Matter Equally
item.description: A submittal date and first energization get the same diamond on the schedule. They are not the same. Miss the freeze-up window and you lose a season. Miss an internal rough-in target by three days…

item.title: Treat Suppliers Like Part of the Team
item.description: Suppliers know when your "drop-dead" date has two weeks of padding in it. Lie to them and they stop telling you about the problems in their shop until it's too late to work around them.

item.title: Use Your Own People Before Consultants
item.description: A consultant at $350 an hour spends the first month learning what your superintendent already knows: which permits are slow, which substation feeds what, why the north yard floods in spring. Then…

item.title: Give Everyone a Desk and a Locker
item.description: If someone keeps their tools in their truck and does paperwork on a gangbox, you've told them they're temporary. Most people act accordingly.

item.title: Collect Status Through the Timesheet
item.description: Status forms are optional, so they don't get filled in. Timesheets always do, because people want to be paid.

item.title: The Two-Hour Wall
item.description: The fire code requires a two-hour wall. That requirement gets copied into the design basis, a wall type, a firestop detail, a QC record and a commissioning check. Then the project closes out and…

item.title: Recurring Work Gets Lost in One Long Bar
item.description: Weekly scaffold inspections show up as one 200-day bar. The bar can't be late, so nobody notices when this week's inspection is.

item.title: Phones Cost Less Than Crew Time
item.description: A crew-hour costs more than a phone. Yet field data still gets written on paper, carried to the trailer and typed in after the crew goes home.

item.title: Add Reversibility to Risk
item.description: Safety learned to put attention on what can kill people, not on what happens often. Project risk can borrow that.

item.title: Track Minor Injuries Too
item.description: Minor cuts and strains go unreported because reporting takes longer than the bandage. If logging one takes more than ten seconds, you'll have no data.

item.title: Crews Are More Than Headcount
item.description: The plan prices six welders at a rate. A crew that has worked together all season outperforms six welders who met on Monday, at the same rate.

item.title: Plan With Weather Data
item.description: Weather is the only project risk with a free, public, daily probabilistic forecast. Most schedules still plan a February pour like a June one.

item.title: Count How Fast You Find New Problems
item.description: You can't list your unknown unknowns. You can count how many new constraints turn up each week.

item.title: Track Material at Every Handoff
item.description: A pipe spool is fabricated, shipped, received, staged and installed, and each of those steps is in a different system. Finding it still takes three phone calls.

item.title: Diagrams Should Come From the Plan
item.description: A roadmap drawn by hand has boxes without dates, arrows without logic and no owners. Nobody can check it, so nobody can prove it wrong. That's why it survives.

item.title: Short Videos Settle Disputes
item.description: Half of all claims are arguments about what the work area looked like on a given date. Thirty seconds of video taken that day ends the argument.

item.title: Make Signatures Quick and Traceable
item.description: A hold-point signature can mean a drive across site, a binder and a wet pen. So people batch them, or sign without looking, and a signature stops meaning much.

item.title: Record Delegation With an End Date
item.description: Who can sign for whom is usually known to two people and an out-of-office reply. When the signer goes on holiday, the job finds out at the first stalled hold point.

item.title: Write Procedures as Steps, Not PDFs
item.description: A procedure in a PDF is advice. The crew carries out a sequence of steps, checks, hold points and qualifications, whatever the document looks like.

item.title: Which Constraint Should We Clear Today?
item.description: Status meetings ask what happened yesterday. The useful question is which blocked item, if cleared today, frees up the most work.

item.title: The Critical Path Changes
item.description: Run a schedule through a thousand simulations of weather and deliveries and a different path is critical in about a third of them. The printed critical path is one of those outcomes.

item.title: Give Assumptions a Recheck Date
item.description: Ground conditions, vendor capacity, "the permit will renew": written down at sanction and never read again. An assumption is a risk nobody has checked yet.

item.title: Baselines Go Stale
item.description: Two winters and forty change orders after sanction, the job is still measured against the sanction-day plan, and the gap is called variance.

item.title: The Whiteboard and the Schedule Drift Apart
item.description: The schedule has five thousand activities. The site runs off a whiteboard three weeks deep, updated at 6 a.m. Both are needed: the contract needs the full record, and the crew needs this week.

item.title: Everything Is a Constraint
item.description: A predecessor, a missing spool, an unsigned permit, a crane booked elsewhere, wind over the lift limit, a room too crowded to work in, a dose budget nearly spent. Seven systems manage them. They're…

item.title: Watch for Closing Windows
item.description: A pour needs three dry days. The crane leaves in October. In-water work stops when the fish return. None of these are logic ties, and most schedules don't model them.

item.title: Some Resources Are Specific People
item.description: The schedule says two Class B welders. The job needs Dave, the only one qualified on that alloy, and Dave is at his daughter's wedding until Tuesday.

item.title: Capture Field Notes Once, in a Usable Shape
item.description: Foremen write down what happened every day. Then the same facts get retyped into the schedule update, the timesheet, an RFI, a QC record and, years later, a claim.

item.title: Use One Breakdown Structure
item.description: The estimate, schedule, cost report and work packages each have a breakdown structure. They match on sanction day. By month six there are four versions and a standing meeting to reconcile them.

item.title: Put a Name on Every Green Status
item.description: Anyone can mark a status green, so reports drift optimistic. Often green just means nobody wanted the argument.

item.title: Measure How Certain the Forecast Is
item.description: SPI and CPI measure work done against the plan. Nothing measures how well we know the finish date, which is what the owner is paying for. A job can report green every month while it gets later.
